Compound disturbance, additively modelled

Testing whether beetle mortality and fire severity interact, in the landscape and in the model, Darkwoods Conservation Area, British Columbia

Author

Seamus Murphy

Published

August 3, 2026

Abstract

Provisional, and deliberately outcome-neutral until the interaction test has run. Compound disturbance is routinely described as an interaction and routinely modelled as a sum. This study separates the two claims over a mountain pine beetle outbreak and the mixed-severity wildfire that followed it in the southern Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia, asking first whether the two agents are associated on the ground and second whether their effects on conifer regeneration multiply or merely add. The first result is negative and concerns the data rather than the forest. The annual beetle classifications from which every beetle surface in the parent study descends were clipped to the fire perimeter before any classification was run, so they carry nodata across almost all of the surrounding unburned forest. The published red-attack surface is confined more tightly still, to the ground where burn severity was classified, and reports beetle attack in no cell outside it. Read at face value that implies almost no beetle mortality in the forest around the fire. The provincial Aerial Overview Survey, an independent record that was never clipped, reports beetle attack outside the perimeter at a rate no lower than inside it, and the small sliver of annual data that does extend beyond the perimeter agrees with the survey rather than with the published surface. Any burned against unburned contrast therefore measures the clip. What survives is the gradient within the perimeter, where every severity class is observed and equally exposed to the clip, and there the corrected grey-stage union, the published red-stage surface and the independent survey all agree that attack peaks at moderate severity rather than rising monotonically. Question A is accordingly reframed as a within-burn question, and the interaction test on regeneration is unaffected.

Keywords

compound disturbance, mountain pine beetle, burn severity, interaction terms, data provenance, analysis extent

1 Introduction

Mountain pine beetle outbreak and wildfire increasingly overlap in the conifer forests of western North America, and the overlap is usually described in the language of interaction. Whether the description is earned is a separate question from whether it is common. Talucci & Krawchuk (2019) and Meigs, Kennedy, & Cohen (2011) both frame the beetle to fire sequence as a modification of fuels and therefore of subsequent severity, and Krawchuk et al. (2020) place compound disturbance at the centre of the refugia concept. The claim that the agents interact is, in each case, a claim about a product rather than a sum.

The parent study for this analysis (Murphy, Leslie, Wilson, & Banks, 2026) modelled conifer regeneration across three four-hectare plots inside the 2015 Mt Midgeley burn, using classified Landsat surfaces for burn severity and for red-stage beetle mortality. Its abstract describes the additive effects of increasing beetle to fire disturbance interactions. Its model, however, enters red attack, grey attack and burn severity as additive main effects with no product term among them. The two statements are not the same statement, and the ambiguity was noticed at the time without being resolved.

This study asks the two questions that separation implies.

The first is whether prior beetle mortality is associated with subsequent burn severity in this landscape. The outbreak ran from 2005 to 2014 and the fire burned in 2015, so the causal arrow runs one way only, from beetle to fire, and never the reverse. The literature on the question is contested rather than empty, so what novelty there is rests on the particular landscape and on the treatment of confounding rather than on the question being new.

The second is whether beetle and fire act additively on regeneration or interact. Here the test is direct: refit the published point process model with the beetle by fire product term and compare it against the published additive fit.

The first question turned out to require a prior question, which is whether the surfaces that would answer it can answer it. Section 3 reports that check. It is negative, it is decisive, and it changes the shape of question one before any ecology is attempted.

2 Materials

2.1 Study area and disturbance history

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the southern Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. A mountain pine beetle outbreak affected the property through the decade to 2014, and the Mt Midgeley wildfire burned part of it in 2015, producing a mixed-severity mosaic. The beetle to fire interval across the burned area ranges from one to eleven years with a median of seven (Murphy et al., 2026).

2.2 Local classified surfaces

G   <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Elevation.utm.tif"))
red <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif"))
sev  <- rast(dpath("fire_severity",  "Fire.Severity.NDBR.tif"))
grey <- rast(file.path(GREY_FIX, "rasters", "mpb_grey_corrected.tif"))
per  <- project(vect(dpath("fire_perimiter", "Fire.Perimiter.shp")), crs(G))

footprint <- function(nm, r) {
  e <- as.vector(ext(r))
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         Rows = nrow(r), Cols = ncol(r),
         `Cell (m)` = round(res(r)[1], 2),
         `Width (km)` = round((e[2] - e[1]) / 1000, 2),
         `Height (km)` = round((e[4] - e[3]) / 1000, 2),
         `Extent (km2)` = round((e[2] - e[1]) * (e[4] - e[3]) / 1e6, 2))
}

FOOT <- bind_rows(
  footprint("Elevation, terrain grid", G),
  footprint("Beetle red stage",        red),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, corrected", grey),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, deprecated", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.GreyStage.tif"))),
  footprint("Beetle continuous (spatstat)", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "MPB.classified.spatstat.tif"))),
  footprint("Burn severity, classified", sev),
  footprint("Beetle by fire intersection", rast(dpath("beetle_fire_interactive", "mpbred_firehigh.tif"))))

PERIM_KM2 <- as.numeric(sum(expanse(per, unit = "km")))
RECT_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Beetle red stage"]
GRID_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Elevation, terrain grid"]

kable(keep(FOOT, "tbl-footprints"), align = "lrrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The fire perimeter encloses 4.8 km2. The beetle red-stage raster spans a rectangle of 7.78 km2 around it, so the raster carries roughly 2.98 km2 of ground outside the burn on which beetle attack could in principle have been mapped. The terrain grid covers 280 km2 of the same landscape and shows what surrounds the burn.

2.3 The severity classes, decoded

The classified severity raster carries integer codes that are not ordered by severity, and the ordering matters to every table that follows. It is established here from the three binary class masks rather than assumed.

P <- rasterize(per, sev, background = 0)

DEC <- lapply(c(High = "High", Moderate = "Med", Low = "Low"), function(cl) {
  m  <- rast(dpath("fire_severity", paste0("Fire.", cl, ".NDBR.tif")))
  cd <- unique(values(sev)[, 1][values(m)[, 1] == 1])
  tibble(Class = cl, Code = cd, Cells = sum(values(m)[, 1] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows()
DEC$Class <- c("High", "Moderate", "Low")

## the two codes that no class mask claims
unclaimed <- setdiff(na.omit(unique(values(sev)[, 1])), DEC$Code)
UNC <- tibble(
  Class = ifelse(sapply(unclaimed, function(k)
            mean(values(P)[, 1][values(sev)[, 1] == k] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)) > 0.5,
          "Inside perimeter, unclassified", "Outside perimeter"),
  Code  = unclaimed,
  Cells = sapply(unclaimed, function(k) sum(values(sev)[, 1] == k, na.rm = TRUE)))

DECODE <- bind_rows(UNC, DEC) |>
  mutate(`Inside perimeter (%)` = round(100 * sapply(Code, function(k)
           mean(values(P)[, 1][values(sev)[, 1] == k] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)) |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Outside perimeter", "Inside perimeter, unclassified",
                         "Low", "Moderate", "High")))

## The mapping is load-bearing. Assert it rather than trusting the read.
stopifnot(DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "High"] == 1,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Low"] == 32,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Moderate"] == 34)
CODE_OF <- setNames(DECODE$Code, DECODE$Class)

kable(keep(DECODE, "tbl-decode"), align = "lrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

Code 1 is high severity and code 34 is moderate, so a table built on the numeric order of the codes would report the two most severe classes the wrong way round. Code 16 is the class that no severity mask claims: 1,268 cells lying inside the fire perimeter but assigned to none of high, moderate or low.

2.4 The independent record

The provincial Aerial Overview Survey is the operational record of forest health in British Columbia. Observers sketch-map damage annually from fixed-wing aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species (Province of British Columbia, Ministry of Forests, 2026). It is coarse, it is observer data, and its errors are positional and perceptual rather than spectral. That last property is what makes it useful here: whatever is wrong with it is uncorrelated with the Landsat classification whose footprint is under test.

## Read with an extent filter built in BC Albers; the provincial layer is
## memory-hostile whole. Project after filtering, never before.
e3005 <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005")
aos   <- vect(AOS_GDB, layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = ext(e3005))
AOS_ALL <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM" & aos$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]
AOS_N <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- project(aos, crs(G))

Over the terrain grid the survey holds 608 damage polygons of all agents and years, of which 276 are mountain pine beetle within the 2005 to 2014 outbreak window used here.

3 The provenance of the beetle layers

The scoping for this study reported a contingency table in which beetle red attack rose from near zero in unburned forest to roughly a fifth of cells at moderate burn severity. Taken at face value that is a strong compound-disturbance signal. It is also exactly the pattern a clipped raster would manufacture, and the clip is the first thing to rule out.

3.1 Where the beetle rasters stop

Pr <- rasterize(per, red, background = 0)
INPER <- values(Pr)[, 1] == 1
CELLS_OUT <- sum(!INPER)
N_RED <- sum(values(red)[, 1] == 1)

## A cell is observed if any annual raster in the outbreak window carries data
## there. -128 and 128 are the nodata sentinels these files use alongside NA.
is_obs <- function(f) { v <- values(rast(f))[, 1]; !(is.na(v) | v == -128 | v == 128) }
OBS <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(ANN, is_obs))

stop_at <- function(nm, present, note) {
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         `Cells present` = sum(present),
         `Inside perimeter` = sum(present & INPER),
         `Outside perimeter` = sum(present & !INPER),
         Note = note)
}

STOPS <- bind_rows(
  stop_at("Annual rasters, any data", OBS, "nodata over the rest"),
  stop_at("Corrected grey stage, 2005 to 2011", values(grey)[, 1] > 0, "union of code 44"),
  stop_at("Red stage, as published", values(red)[, 1] == 1, "substituted for a missing layer"))

OBS_OUT   <- sum(OBS & !INPER)
GREY_OUT  <- sum(values(grey)[, 1] > 0 & !INPER)
RED_OUT   <- sum(values(red)[, 1] == 1 & !INPER)
PCT_OBS_OUT <- 100 * OBS_OUT / CELLS_OUT

kable(keep(STOPS, "tbl-perimeter"), align = "lrrrl") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The annual rasters carry data on 0.3 per cent of the 3,429 cells lying outside the fire perimeter, and nodata on the rest. Every beetle surface in the study descends from those files, so every one of them inherits the boundary: the corrected grey union places 1 of its 1541 cells outside the perimeter and the published red-stage surface places 0 of its 493.

The clip is in the source data, not in any downstream step. All nine annual files carry an identical nodata count, and the boundary it traces is the fire perimeter, which is a shape no property of beetle ecology would produce. Whoever prepared the time series clipped it to the burn before the classification that used it was ever run.

3.2 Two nested masks, not one

The red and grey surfaces do not stop in the same place, and the difference matters.

SEV <- resample(sev, red, method = "near")
CLASSIFIED <- values(SEV)[, 1] %in% CODE_OF[c("Low", "Moderate", "High")]

NEST <- tibble(
  Region = c("Outside the fire perimeter",
             "Inside perimeter, unclassified severity",
             "Inside the classified severity footprint"),
  Cells = c(CELLS_OUT, sum(INPER & !CLASSIFIED), sum(CLASSIFIED)),
  `Annual data (%)` = round(100 * c(mean(OBS[!INPER]), mean(OBS[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                    mean(OBS[CLASSIFIED])), 1),
  `Grey attack (%)` = round(100 * c(mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[!INPER]),
                                    mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                    mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[CLASSIFIED])), 1),
  `Red attack (%)` = round(100 * c(mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[!INPER]),
                                   mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                   mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[CLASSIFIED])), 1))

kable(keep(NEST, "tbl-nested"), align = "lrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

Inside the perimeter but outside the classified severity footprint, the annual rasters are 99.7 per cent observed and the corrected grey union records attack in 33.1 per cent of cells. The published red-stage surface records it in 0 per cent. That contrast cannot be ecological: the same ground, in the same years, is either a third attacked or not attacked at all depending on which derivative of the same annual files is consulted.

So there are two clips, one inside the other. The annual series is clipped to the fire perimeter, and Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif is confined more tightly still, to the ground where burn severity was classified. The narrower one is an accident of substitution rather than a decision: the layer the published analysis intended to use, mpb_red_na.tif, is missing from the repository, and Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif was put in its place (Murphy, 2026a).

3.3 The same test against the independent survey

If the zeroes are ecological, the provincial survey should also find little beetle attack outside the burn. If they are clipping, the survey should find as much there as anywhere. The small sliver of annual data that does extend beyond the perimeter provides a second, internal check on the same question.

A  <- rasterize(aos, red, background = 0)
EL <- resample(G, red)

## Class on the perimeter first, then on severity within it. Keying this table on
## the severity code alone would put 67 in-perimeter cells that the severity
## raster codes 0 into the "outside" row and inflate what little the local data
## says out there by a factor of seven.
CC <- tibble(sev = values(SEV)[, 1], grey = values(grey)[, 1] > 0,
             red = values(red)[, 1] == 1, aos = values(A)[, 1] == 1,
             elev = values(EL)[, 1], obs = OBS, inper = INPER) |>
  mutate(Class = ifelse(!inper, "Outside perimeter",
                 ifelse(sev %in% CODE_OF[c("Low", "Moderate", "High")],
                        names(CODE_OF)[match(sev, CODE_OF)],
                        "Inside perimeter, unclassified"))) |>
  group_by(Class) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(),
            `Observed (%)` = round(100 * mean(obs), 1),
            Observed = sum(obs),
            `Grey (%)` = round(100 * mean(grey[obs]), 1),
            `Red (%)`  = round(100 * mean(red[obs]), 1),
            `Survey (%)` = round(100 * mean(aos), 1),
            `Elevation (m)` = round(mean(elev, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Outside perimeter", "Inside perimeter, unclassified",
                         "Low", "Moderate", "High")))

OUTROW <- CC |> filter(Class == "Outside perimeter")
BURNED <- CC |> filter(Class %in% c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

kable(keep(CC, "tbl-crosscheck"), align = "lrrrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(which(CC$Class == "Outside perimeter"), background = "#f7e7e7")

The shaded row carries the argument. Outside the fire perimeter the survey records 40.4 per cent of the ground as attacked, a rate no lower than anything inside the burn and higher than two of the three burned classes. The local surfaces report nothing there at all, and they report nothing because they see nothing: of 3,429 cells outside the perimeter the annual rasters observe 10.

That figure is worth stating plainly rather than converting to a rate. The local record is not sparse outside the burn, it is very nearly absent, and 10 cells cannot corroborate or contradict anything. The comparison therefore rests on the survey alone, which is sufficient: an independent census of the same ground in the same years finds beetle attack there in ordinary abundance. The zero the published red-stage surface reports outside the burn is a statement about the extent of the file, not about the forest.

perim_sf <- st_as_sf(per)

## Relabel each surface from its raw codes so the legends carry meaning rather
## than integers. Cells shown white are outside the fire perimeter entirely.
relabel <- function(r, from, to) {
  out <- r
  values(out) <- factor(to[match(values(r)[, 1], from)], levels = to)
  out
}
panel <- function(r, title, pal) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    geom_sf(data = perim_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey15", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal, na.value = "white", name = NULL,
                      na.translate = FALSE, drop = FALSE) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
    labs(title = title) +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9, hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(9, "pt"),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
          legend.margin = margin(t = 2, b = 0))
}

SEV_ORDER <- c("Inside perimeter, unclassified", "Low", "Moderate", "High")
sev_lab <- SEV
values(sev_lab)[values(sev_lab)[, 1] == CODE_OF[["Outside perimeter"]]] <- NA
sev_lab <- relabel(sev_lab, CODE_OF[SEV_ORDER], SEV_ORDER)

## Unobserved cells are shown as a class of their own rather than as absence.
beetle_panel <- function(r, title, hit, col) {
  x <- r
  values(x) <- factor(ifelse(!OBS, "Not observed",
                      ifelse(values(r)[, 1] %in% hit, "Attack", "No attack")),
                      levels = c("Not observed", "No attack", "Attack"))
  panel(x, title, c(`Not observed` = "white", `No attack` = "grey88", Attack = col))
}

p1 <- beetle_panel(red,  "Red stage, as published",      1, "#b2182b")
p2 <- beetle_panel(grey, "Grey stage, corrected 2026-06-02", 1, "#7b3294")
p3 <- panel(sev_lab, "Burn severity classes",
            setNames(c("grey70", "#fddbc7", "#ef8a62", "#67001f"), SEV_ORDER))
p4 <- panel(relabel(A, c(0, 1), c("Not attacked", "Beetle attack")),
            "Aerial Overview Survey, beetle",
            c(`Not attacked` = "grey88", `Beetle attack` = "#2166ac"))

FIG_MASK <- (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
ggsave(file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-mask.png"), FIG_MASK,
       width = 9, height = 9.6, dpi = 300)
FIG_MASK

3.4 What survives

The clip destroys any comparison that crosses the fire perimeter and leaves untouched any comparison made entirely inside it. The three severity classes all sit within the perimeter and are observed at better than 100 per cent, so the clip cannot generate differences among them.

WB <- BURNED |>
  select(Class, Cells, `Grey (%)`, `Red (%)`, `Survey (%)`, `Elevation (m)`) |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Low", "Moderate", "High")))
shape <- function(col) paste(sprintf("%.1f", WB[[col]]), collapse = ", ")
PEAKS <- vapply(c("Grey (%)", "Red (%)", "Survey (%)"),
                function(k) WB$Class[which.max(WB[[k]])], character(1))
stopifnot(length(unique(PEAKS)) == 1L)
kable(keep(WB, "tbl-withinburn"), align = "lrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

Three records agree on the shape. The corrected grey union runs 20.8, 34.6, 27.7 per cent across low, moderate and high severity, the published red-stage surface 6.3, 20.7, 12.1, and the independent survey 24.5, 40.6, 33.1. All three peak at moderate and fall at high, and the assertion above fails the render if they ever stop agreeing. The two local surfaces share a measurement pathway with each other but not with the survey, so the agreement is not one instrument repeating itself.

That agreement is not yet evidence about fire. The elevation column is the reason. Moderate severity occupies the highest mean elevation of the three burned classes at 1449 m, and the companion refugia analysis of this landscape finds beetle attack peaking near 1,430 m for reasons that have nothing to do with fire (Murphy, 2026b). A severity gradient that is also an elevation gradient will reproduce the beetle elevation optimum whether or not severity matters. Conditioning on host abundance and on elevation is therefore the first task of the next phase, not a robustness check appended to it.

4 Status and next steps

This document is a Phase 0 draft. It reports the provenance check and nothing further, because the check governs what the rest of the study is permitted to ask.

Question A, as originally posed, compared burned against unburned ground and cannot be asked of these surfaces. It is reframed as a within-burn question about the severity gradient, which the clip does not touch and on which three records agree. Recovering the original comparison would mean rebuilding the classification over the unclipped landscape from the Landsat archive, which is a reprocessing task rather than an analysis task, and it would re-tread the parent study’s published methods.

Two things follow for the analysis that comes next. The corrected grey-stage union of 2 June 2026 (Murphy, 2026a) should be preferred to the published red-stage surface wherever either would serve, because it is three times denser, it is observed throughout the perimeter rather than only where severity was classified, and its derivation is documented. And the missing mpb_red_na.tif should be looked for before the red-stage surface is used again, since the substitution that replaced it is the narrower of the two clips.

Question B is untouched. The regeneration response, the seedling point pattern, lies wholly within the burn, so every cell entering the point process model sits inside the clip and is equally affected by it. Refitting the published additive model with the beetle by fire product term remains the direct test, and it is the next phase of work.

abstract: >
  Provisional, and deliberately outcome-neutral until the interaction test has run. Compound
  disturbance is routinely described as an interaction and routinely modelled as a sum. This study
  separates the two claims over a mountain pine beetle outbreak and the mixed-severity wildfire that
  followed it in the southern Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia, asking first whether the two
  agents are associated on the ground and second whether their effects on conifer regeneration
  multiply or merely add. The first result is negative and concerns the data rather
  than the forest. The annual beetle classifications from which every beetle surface in the parent
  study descends were clipped to the fire perimeter before any classification was run, so they
  carry nodata across almost all of the surrounding unburned forest. The published red-attack
  surface is confined more tightly still, to the ground where burn severity was classified, and
  reports beetle attack in no cell outside it. Read at face value that implies almost no beetle
  mortality in the forest around the fire. The provincial Aerial Overview Survey, an independent
  record that was never clipped, reports beetle attack outside the perimeter at a rate no lower
  than inside it, and the small sliver of annual data that does extend beyond the perimeter agrees
  with the survey rather than with the published surface. Any burned against unburned contrast
  therefore measures the clip. What survives is the gradient within the perimeter, where every
  severity class is observed and equally exposed to the clip, and there the corrected grey-stage
  union, the published red-stage surface and the independent survey all agree that attack peaks at
  moderate severity rather than rising monotonically. Question A is accordingly reframed as a
  within-burn question, and the interaction test on regeneration is unaffected.
keywords:
  - compound disturbance
  - mountain pine beetle
  - burn severity
  - interaction terms
  - data provenance
  - analysis extent

# Introduction

Mountain pine beetle outbreak and wildfire increasingly overlap in the conifer forests of western North America, and the overlap is usually described in the language of interaction. Whether the description is earned is a separate question from whether it is common. @talucci2019dead and @meigs2011 both frame the beetle to fire sequence as a modification of fuels and therefore of subsequent severity, and @krawchuk2020 place compound disturbance at the centre of the refugia concept. The claim that the agents interact is, in each case, a claim about a product rather than a sum.

The parent study for this analysis [@murphy2026] modelled conifer regeneration across three four-hectare plots inside the 2015 Mt Midgeley burn, using classified Landsat surfaces for burn severity and for red-stage beetle mortality. Its abstract describes the additive effects of increasing beetle to fire disturbance interactions. Its model, however, enters red attack, grey attack and burn severity as additive main effects with no product term among them. The two statements are not the same statement, and the ambiguity was noticed at the time without being resolved.

This study asks the two questions that separation implies.

The first is whether prior beetle mortality is associated with subsequent burn severity in this landscape. The outbreak ran from 2005 to 2014 and the fire burned in 2015, so the causal arrow runs one way only, from beetle to fire, and never the reverse. The literature on the question is contested rather than empty, so what novelty there is rests on the particular landscape and on the treatment of confounding rather than on the question being new.

The second is whether beetle and fire act additively on regeneration or interact. Here the test is direct: refit the published point process model with the beetle by fire product term and compare it against the published additive fit.

The first question turned out to require a prior question, which is whether the surfaces that would answer it can answer it. @sec-provenance reports that check. It is negative, it is decisive, and it changes the shape of question one before any ecology is attempted.

# Materials

## Study area and disturbance history {#sec-area}

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the southern Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. A mountain pine beetle outbreak affected the property through the decade to 2014, and the Mt Midgeley wildfire burned part of it in 2015, producing a mixed-severity mosaic. The beetle to fire interval across the burned area ranges from one to eleven years with a median of seven [@murphy2026].

## Local classified surfaces {#sec-local}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-footprints
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Footprints of the local classified surfaces against the terrain grid. Every disturbance surface is confined to a rectangle of roughly eight square kilometres; the terrain grid covers thirty-four times that area."

G   <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Elevation.utm.tif"))
red <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif"))
sev  <- rast(dpath("fire_severity",  "Fire.Severity.NDBR.tif"))
grey <- rast(file.path(GREY_FIX, "rasters", "mpb_grey_corrected.tif"))
per  <- project(vect(dpath("fire_perimiter", "Fire.Perimiter.shp")), crs(G))

footprint <- function(nm, r) {
  e <- as.vector(ext(r))
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         Rows = nrow(r), Cols = ncol(r),
         `Cell (m)` = round(res(r)[1], 2),
         `Width (km)` = round((e[2] - e[1]) / 1000, 2),
         `Height (km)` = round((e[4] - e[3]) / 1000, 2),
         `Extent (km2)` = round((e[2] - e[1]) * (e[4] - e[3]) / 1e6, 2))
}

FOOT <- bind_rows(
  footprint("Elevation, terrain grid", G),
  footprint("Beetle red stage",        red),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, corrected", grey),
  footprint("Beetle grey stage, deprecated", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Outbreak.GreyStage.tif"))),
  footprint("Beetle continuous (spatstat)", rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "MPB.classified.spatstat.tif"))),
  footprint("Burn severity, classified", sev),
  footprint("Beetle by fire intersection", rast(dpath("beetle_fire_interactive", "mpbred_firehigh.tif"))))

PERIM_KM2 <- as.numeric(sum(expanse(per, unit = "km")))
RECT_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Beetle red stage"]
GRID_KM2  <- FOOT$`Extent (km2)`[FOOT$Surface == "Elevation, terrain grid"]

kable(keep(FOOT, "tbl-footprints"), align = "lrrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The fire perimeter encloses `r round(PERIM_KM2, 2)` km^2^. The beetle red-stage raster spans a rectangle of `r RECT_KM2` km^2^ around it, so the raster carries roughly `r round(RECT_KM2 - PERIM_KM2, 2)` km^2^ of ground outside the burn on which beetle attack could in principle have been mapped. The terrain grid covers `r round(GRID_KM2, 0)` km^2^ of the same landscape and shows what surrounds the burn.

## The severity classes, decoded {#sec-decode}

The classified severity raster carries integer codes that are not ordered by severity, and the ordering matters to every table that follows. It is established here from the three binary class masks rather than assumed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-decode
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Decoding the classified burn severity raster against its own binary class masks, and against the fire perimeter. The integer codes are not in severity order. Code 16 falls inside the perimeter but in none of the three severity classes."

P <- rasterize(per, sev, background = 0)

DEC <- lapply(c(High = "High", Moderate = "Med", Low = "Low"), function(cl) {
  m  <- rast(dpath("fire_severity", paste0("Fire.", cl, ".NDBR.tif")))
  cd <- unique(values(sev)[, 1][values(m)[, 1] == 1])
  tibble(Class = cl, Code = cd, Cells = sum(values(m)[, 1] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows()
DEC$Class <- c("High", "Moderate", "Low")

## the two codes that no class mask claims
unclaimed <- setdiff(na.omit(unique(values(sev)[, 1])), DEC$Code)
UNC <- tibble(
  Class = ifelse(sapply(unclaimed, function(k)
            mean(values(P)[, 1][values(sev)[, 1] == k] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)) > 0.5,
          "Inside perimeter, unclassified", "Outside perimeter"),
  Code  = unclaimed,
  Cells = sapply(unclaimed, function(k) sum(values(sev)[, 1] == k, na.rm = TRUE)))

DECODE <- bind_rows(UNC, DEC) |>
  mutate(`Inside perimeter (%)` = round(100 * sapply(Code, function(k)
           mean(values(P)[, 1][values(sev)[, 1] == k] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)) |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Outside perimeter", "Inside perimeter, unclassified",
                         "Low", "Moderate", "High")))

## The mapping is load-bearing. Assert it rather than trusting the read.
stopifnot(DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "High"] == 1,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Low"] == 32,
          DEC$Code[DEC$Class == "Moderate"] == 34)
CODE_OF <- setNames(DECODE$Code, DECODE$Class)

kable(keep(DECODE, "tbl-decode"), align = "lrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Code 1 is high severity and code 34 is moderate, so a table built on the numeric order of the codes would report the two most severe classes the wrong way round. Code 16 is the class that no severity mask claims: `r format(DECODE$Cells[DECODE$Class == "Inside perimeter, unclassified"], big.mark = ",")` cells lying inside the fire perimeter but assigned to none of high, moderate or low.

## The independent record {#sec-aos}

The provincial Aerial Overview Survey is the operational record of forest health in British Columbia. Observers sketch-map damage annually from fixed-wing aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species [@bcaos2026]. It is coarse, it is observer data, and its errors are positional and perceptual rather than spectral. That last property is what makes it useful here: whatever is wrong with it is uncorrelated with the Landsat classification whose footprint is under test.

```{r}
#| label: aos
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Read with an extent filter built in BC Albers; the provincial layer is
## memory-hostile whole. Project after filtering, never before.
e3005 <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005")
aos   <- vect(AOS_GDB, layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = ext(e3005))
AOS_ALL <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM" & aos$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]
AOS_N <- nrow(aos)
aos   <- project(aos, crs(G))
```

Over the terrain grid the survey holds `r format(AOS_ALL, big.mark = ",")` damage polygons of all agents and years, of which `r AOS_N` are mountain pine beetle within the `r min(OUTBREAK)` to `r max(OUTBREAK)` outbreak window used here.

# The provenance of the beetle layers {#sec-provenance}

The scoping for this study reported a contingency table in which beetle red attack rose from near
zero in unburned forest to roughly a fifth of cells at moderate burn severity. Taken at face value
that is a strong compound-disturbance signal. It is also exactly the pattern a clipped raster would
manufacture, and the clip is the first thing to rule out.

## Where the beetle rasters stop {#sec-perimeter}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-perimeter
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Where each beetle surface stops, against the fire perimeter, on the native 29.558 m beetle grid. The annual rasters carry nodata over almost the whole area outside the perimeter, and the two derived surfaces inherit it."

Pr <- rasterize(per, red, background = 0)
INPER <- values(Pr)[, 1] == 1
CELLS_OUT <- sum(!INPER)
N_RED <- sum(values(red)[, 1] == 1)

## A cell is observed if any annual raster in the outbreak window carries data
## there. -128 and 128 are the nodata sentinels these files use alongside NA.
is_obs <- function(f) { v <- values(rast(f))[, 1]; !(is.na(v) | v == -128 | v == 128) }
OBS <- Reduce(`|`, lapply(ANN, is_obs))

stop_at <- function(nm, present, note) {
  tibble(Surface = nm,
         `Cells present` = sum(present),
         `Inside perimeter` = sum(present & INPER),
         `Outside perimeter` = sum(present & !INPER),
         Note = note)
}

STOPS <- bind_rows(
  stop_at("Annual rasters, any data", OBS, "nodata over the rest"),
  stop_at("Corrected grey stage, 2005 to 2011", values(grey)[, 1] > 0, "union of code 44"),
  stop_at("Red stage, as published", values(red)[, 1] == 1, "substituted for a missing layer"))

OBS_OUT   <- sum(OBS & !INPER)
GREY_OUT  <- sum(values(grey)[, 1] > 0 & !INPER)
RED_OUT   <- sum(values(red)[, 1] == 1 & !INPER)
PCT_OBS_OUT <- 100 * OBS_OUT / CELLS_OUT

kable(keep(STOPS, "tbl-perimeter"), align = "lrrrl") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The annual rasters carry data on `r round(PCT_OBS_OUT, 1)` per cent of the
`r format(CELLS_OUT, big.mark = ",")` cells lying outside the fire perimeter, and nodata on the
rest. Every beetle surface in the study descends from those files, so every one of them inherits the
boundary: the corrected grey union places `r GREY_OUT` of its `r sum(values(grey)[, 1] > 0)` cells
outside the perimeter and the published red-stage surface places `r RED_OUT` of its `r N_RED`.

**The clip is in the source data, not in any downstream step.** All nine annual files carry an
identical nodata count, and the boundary it traces is the fire perimeter, which is a shape no
property of beetle ecology would produce. Whoever prepared the time series clipped it to the burn
before the classification that used it was ever run.

## Two nested masks, not one {#sec-nested}

The red and grey surfaces do not stop in the same place, and the difference matters.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nested
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The two surfaces against the classified severity footprint. Grey attack is recorded throughout the perimeter; red attack is confined to the three classified severity classes and is absent from the 1,268 cells inside the perimeter that no class mask claims."

SEV <- resample(sev, red, method = "near")
CLASSIFIED <- values(SEV)[, 1] %in% CODE_OF[c("Low", "Moderate", "High")]

NEST <- tibble(
  Region = c("Outside the fire perimeter",
             "Inside perimeter, unclassified severity",
             "Inside the classified severity footprint"),
  Cells = c(CELLS_OUT, sum(INPER & !CLASSIFIED), sum(CLASSIFIED)),
  `Annual data (%)` = round(100 * c(mean(OBS[!INPER]), mean(OBS[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                    mean(OBS[CLASSIFIED])), 1),
  `Grey attack (%)` = round(100 * c(mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[!INPER]),
                                    mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                    mean((values(grey)[, 1] > 0)[CLASSIFIED])), 1),
  `Red attack (%)` = round(100 * c(mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[!INPER]),
                                   mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[INPER & !CLASSIFIED]),
                                   mean((values(red)[, 1] == 1)[CLASSIFIED])), 1))

kable(keep(NEST, "tbl-nested"), align = "lrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Inside the perimeter but outside the classified severity footprint, the annual rasters are
`r NEST$"Annual data (%)"[2]` per cent observed and the corrected grey union records attack in
`r NEST$"Grey attack (%)"[2]` per cent of cells. The published red-stage surface records it in
`r NEST$"Red attack (%)"[2]` per cent. That contrast cannot be ecological: the same ground, in the
same years, is either a third attacked or not attacked at all depending on which derivative of the
same annual files is consulted.

So there are two clips, one inside the other. The annual series is clipped to the fire perimeter,
and `Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif` is confined more tightly still, to the ground where burn severity
was classified. The narrower one is an accident of substitution rather than a decision: the layer
the published analysis intended to use, `mpb_red_na.tif`, is missing from the repository, and
`Beetle.Outbreak.RedStage.tif` was put in its place [@murphy2026greyfix].

## The same test against the independent survey {#sec-crosscheck}

If the zeroes are ecological, the provincial survey should also find little beetle attack outside
the burn. If they are clipping, the survey should find as much there as anywhere. The small sliver
of annual data that does extend beyond the perimeter provides a second, internal check on the same
question.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-crosscheck
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The two local surfaces against the independent Aerial Overview Survey, by burn severity class. Local rates are computed only over cells the annual rasters actually observe. The survey finds no shortage of beetle attack outside the burn, and neither does the small observed sliver of the local data."

A  <- rasterize(aos, red, background = 0)
EL <- resample(G, red)

## Class on the perimeter first, then on severity within it. Keying this table on
## the severity code alone would put 67 in-perimeter cells that the severity
## raster codes 0 into the "outside" row and inflate what little the local data
## says out there by a factor of seven.
CC <- tibble(sev = values(SEV)[, 1], grey = values(grey)[, 1] > 0,
             red = values(red)[, 1] == 1, aos = values(A)[, 1] == 1,
             elev = values(EL)[, 1], obs = OBS, inper = INPER) |>
  mutate(Class = ifelse(!inper, "Outside perimeter",
                 ifelse(sev %in% CODE_OF[c("Low", "Moderate", "High")],
                        names(CODE_OF)[match(sev, CODE_OF)],
                        "Inside perimeter, unclassified"))) |>
  group_by(Class) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(),
            `Observed (%)` = round(100 * mean(obs), 1),
            Observed = sum(obs),
            `Grey (%)` = round(100 * mean(grey[obs]), 1),
            `Red (%)`  = round(100 * mean(red[obs]), 1),
            `Survey (%)` = round(100 * mean(aos), 1),
            `Elevation (m)` = round(mean(elev, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Outside perimeter", "Inside perimeter, unclassified",
                         "Low", "Moderate", "High")))

OUTROW <- CC |> filter(Class == "Outside perimeter")
BURNED <- CC |> filter(Class %in% c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

kable(keep(CC, "tbl-crosscheck"), align = "lrrrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) |>
  row_spec(which(CC$Class == "Outside perimeter"), background = "#f7e7e7")
```

The shaded row carries the argument. Outside the fire perimeter the survey records
`r sprintf("%.1f", OUTROW$"Survey (%)")` per cent of the ground as attacked, a rate no lower than
anything inside the burn and higher than two of the three burned classes. The local surfaces report
nothing there at all, and they report nothing because they see nothing: of
`r format(OUTROW$Cells, big.mark = ",")` cells outside the perimeter the annual rasters observe
`r OUTROW$Observed`.

That figure is worth stating plainly rather than converting to a rate. The local record is not
sparse outside the burn, it is very nearly absent, and `r OUTROW$Observed` cells cannot corroborate
or contradict anything. The comparison therefore rests on the survey alone, which is sufficient: an
independent census of the same ground in the same years finds beetle attack there in ordinary
abundance. The zero the published red-stage surface reports outside the burn is a statement about
the extent of the file, not about the forest.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mask
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The clip, mapped. Top left, the published red-stage surface, which stops at the classified burn. Top right, the corrected grey-stage union, which reaches the fire perimeter and stops there. Bottom left, the burn severity classes. Bottom right, the independent Aerial Overview Survey, which does not stop at anything. The unburned ground in the two upper panels is empty because it was never observed, not because it was never attacked."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 9.6

perim_sf <- st_as_sf(per)

## Relabel each surface from its raw codes so the legends carry meaning rather
## than integers. Cells shown white are outside the fire perimeter entirely.
relabel <- function(r, from, to) {
  out <- r
  values(out) <- factor(to[match(values(r)[, 1], from)], levels = to)
  out
}
panel <- function(r, title, pal) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    geom_sf(data = perim_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey15", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal, na.value = "white", name = NULL,
                      na.translate = FALSE, drop = FALSE) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
    labs(title = title) +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          panel.grid = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9, hjust = 0.5),
          legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(9, "pt"),
          legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
          legend.margin = margin(t = 2, b = 0))
}

SEV_ORDER <- c("Inside perimeter, unclassified", "Low", "Moderate", "High")
sev_lab <- SEV
values(sev_lab)[values(sev_lab)[, 1] == CODE_OF[["Outside perimeter"]]] <- NA
sev_lab <- relabel(sev_lab, CODE_OF[SEV_ORDER], SEV_ORDER)

## Unobserved cells are shown as a class of their own rather than as absence.
beetle_panel <- function(r, title, hit, col) {
  x <- r
  values(x) <- factor(ifelse(!OBS, "Not observed",
                      ifelse(values(r)[, 1] %in% hit, "Attack", "No attack")),
                      levels = c("Not observed", "No attack", "Attack"))
  panel(x, title, c(`Not observed` = "white", `No attack` = "grey88", Attack = col))
}

p1 <- beetle_panel(red,  "Red stage, as published",      1, "#b2182b")
p2 <- beetle_panel(grey, "Grey stage, corrected 2026-06-02", 1, "#7b3294")
p3 <- panel(sev_lab, "Burn severity classes",
            setNames(c("grey70", "#fddbc7", "#ef8a62", "#67001f"), SEV_ORDER))
p4 <- panel(relabel(A, c(0, 1), c("Not attacked", "Beetle attack")),
            "Aerial Overview Survey, beetle",
            c(`Not attacked` = "grey88", `Beetle attack` = "#2166ac"))

FIG_MASK <- (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
ggsave(file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-mask.png"), FIG_MASK,
       width = 9, height = 9.6, dpi = 300)
FIG_MASK
```

## What survives {#sec-survives}

The clip destroys any comparison that crosses the fire perimeter and leaves untouched any comparison
made entirely inside it. The three severity classes all sit within the perimeter and are observed at
better than `r floor(min(BURNED$"Observed (%)"))` per cent, so the clip cannot generate differences
among them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-withinburn
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Beetle attack across burn severity within the fire perimeter, in the two local surfaces and in the independent survey. All three peak at moderate severity and fall at high."

WB <- BURNED |>
  select(Class, Cells, `Grey (%)`, `Red (%)`, `Survey (%)`, `Elevation (m)`) |>
  arrange(match(Class, c("Low", "Moderate", "High")))
shape <- function(col) paste(sprintf("%.1f", WB[[col]]), collapse = ", ")
PEAKS <- vapply(c("Grey (%)", "Red (%)", "Survey (%)"),
                function(k) WB$Class[which.max(WB[[k]])], character(1))
stopifnot(length(unique(PEAKS)) == 1L)
kable(keep(WB, "tbl-withinburn"), align = "lrrrrr") |> kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Three records agree on the shape. The corrected grey union runs `r shape("Grey (%)")` per cent
across low, moderate and high severity, the published red-stage surface `r shape("Red (%)")`, and
the independent survey `r shape("Survey (%)")`. All three peak at `r tolower(unique(PEAKS))` and
fall at high, and the assertion above fails the render if they ever stop agreeing. The two local
surfaces share a measurement pathway with each other but not with the survey, so the agreement is
not one instrument repeating itself.

That agreement is not yet evidence about fire. The elevation column is the reason. Moderate severity
occupies the highest mean elevation of the three burned classes at
`r WB$"Elevation (m)"[WB$Class == "Moderate"]` m, and the companion refugia analysis of this
landscape finds beetle attack peaking near 1,430 m for reasons that have nothing to do with fire
[@murphy2026refugia]. A severity gradient that is also an elevation gradient will reproduce the
beetle elevation optimum whether or not severity matters. Conditioning on host abundance and on
elevation is therefore the first task of the next phase, not a robustness check appended to it.

# Status and next steps {#sec-status}

This document is a Phase 0 draft. It reports the provenance check and nothing further, because the check governs what the rest of the study is permitted to ask.

Question A, as originally posed, compared burned against unburned ground and cannot be asked of these surfaces. It is reframed as a within-burn question about the severity gradient, which the clip does not touch and on which three records agree. Recovering the original comparison would mean rebuilding the classification over the unclipped landscape from the Landsat archive, which is a reprocessing task rather than an analysis task, and it would re-tread the parent study's published methods.

Two things follow for the analysis that comes next. The corrected grey-stage union of 2 June 2026 [@murphy2026greyfix] should be preferred to the published red-stage surface wherever either would serve, because it is three times denser, it is observed throughout the perimeter rather than only where severity was classified, and its derivation is documented. And the missing `mpb_red_na.tif` should be looked for before the red-stage surface is used again, since the substitution that replaced it is the narrower of the two clips.

Question B is untouched. The regeneration response, the seedling point pattern, lies wholly within the burn, so every cell entering the point process model sits inside the clip and is equally affected by it. Refitting the published additive model with the beetle by fire product term remains the direct test, and it is the next phase of work.
